{{Short description|Japanese prehistoric mythological event}}
{{italic title}}
{{Shinto}}
The {{Nihongo||国譲り|'''kuni-yuzuri'''|extra2="Transfer of the land"}} was a mythological event in Japanese prehistory, related in sources such as the ''[[Kojiki]]'' and the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]''. It relates the story of how the rulership of Japan passed from the earthly ''[[kami]]'' (''[[kunitsukami]]'') to the ''kami'' of Heaven (''[[amatsukami]]'') and their eventual descendants, the {{ill|Imperial House of Japan|en|Imperial House of Japan|qid=Q909452|lt=Imperial House of Japan|1=Imperial House of Japan}}.{{efn|In Japanese mythology, the gods who reside in the Plain of High Heaven ([[Takamagahara]]) such as Amaterasu are collectively called {{nihongo|''amatsukami''|天津神||"heavenly gods"}}, while the deities who dwell on the earth / the land of Japan ([[:en:Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni|Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni]]) such as Ōkuninushi are called {{nihongo|''kunitsukami''|国津神|1=Kunitsukami||"earthly gods" or "regional gods"}}}}<ref name="shinto-encyclopedia">{{cite web|last1=Kobori|first1=Keiko|title=Kuniyuzuri|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=1210|website=Encyclopedia of Shinto|publisher=Kokugakuin University|access-date=9 March 2017}}</ref>

==Background==
{{see also|Kuniumi|Kamiumi}}

The ''Kojiki'' and the ''Nihon Shoki'' both relate that the [[Japanese archipelago]] were [[Kuniumi|created]] by the primordial couple [[Izanagi]] and {{ill|Izanami|en|Izanami|qid=Q682306|lt=Izanami|1=Izanami}}, who also [[Kamiumi|brought forth]] many gods into existence,<ref>Chamberlain, Basil (1882). [http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj012.htm Section V.—Birth of the Eight Islands.] ''A translation of the "Ko-ji-ki" or Records of Ancient Matters.'' Yokohama: Lane, Crawford & Co.</ref> three of which – [[Amaterasu]], [[Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto|Tsukuyomi]] and [[Susanoo-no-Mikoto|Susanoo]] – were appointed to govern the sky ([[Takamagahara]], the 'Plain of High Heaven'), the night, and the seas, respectively.<ref>Chamberlain (1882). [http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj018.htm Section XI.—Investiture of the Three Deities; The Illustrious August Children.]</ref><ref>{{cite wikisource |Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |chapter=Book I |author=Aston, William George |date=1896 |pages=1–33}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=Mori|first1=Mizue|title=Amaterasu|url=http://k-amc.kokugakuin.ac.jp/DM/dbSearchList.do;jsessionid=734512D3512087B5065364047A4C4B03?class_name=col_eos&search_condition_type=1&db_search_condition_type=0&View=0&focus_type=0&startNo=1&searchFreeword=Amaterasu&searchRangeType=0|website=Encyclopedia of Shinto|publisher=Kokugakuin University}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=Kadoya|first1=Atsushi|title=Susanoo|url=http://k-amc.kokugakuin.ac.jp/DM/dbSearchList.do;jsessionid=734512D3512087B5065364047A4C4B03?class_name=col_eos&search_condition_type=1&db_search_condition_type=0&View=0&focus_type=0&startNo=1&searchFreeword=Susanoo&searchRangeType=0|website=Encyclopedia of Shinto|publisher=Kokugakuin University}}</ref>

Susanoo, expelled by Izanagi either because he refused to perform his allotted task of ruling the sea (''Kojiki'')<ref>Chamberlain (1882). [http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj019.htm Section XII.—The Crying and Weeping of His Impetuous-Male-Augustness.]</ref> or his impetuous nature (''Nihon Shoki''),<ref>{{cite wikisource |Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |chapter=Book I |author=Aston |date=1896 |page=20}}</ref> went to Takamagahara to see his sister. Suspected of insurrection, Susanoo protested his innocence, at which the two gods underwent a trial by pledge,<ref>Chamberlain (1882). [http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj020.htm Section XIII.—The August Oath.]</ref><ref>{{cite wikisource |Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |chapter=Book I |author=Aston |date=1896 |pages=33–35}}</ref> giving birth to five male ''kami'' (Amaterasu's sons) and three female ''kami'' (Susanoo's daughters) when each chewed and spat out an object carried by the other (Amaterasu Susanoo's [[Totsuka-no-Tsurugi|ten-span sword]], Susanoo Amaterasu's ''[[magatama]]'' beads).<ref>Chamberlain (1882). [http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj021.htm Section XIV.—The August Declaration of the Division of the August Male Children and the August Female Children.]</ref><ref>{{cite wikisource |Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |chapter=Book I |author=Aston |date=1896 |pages=35–40}}</ref>

[[File:Meiji standing screen from Crow Collection 02.jpg|thumb|left|180px|[[Susanoo-no-Mikoto|Susanoo]] fighting the {{ill|Yamata no Orochi|en|Yamata no Orochi|qid=Q1054437|lt=Yamata no Orochi|1=Yamata no Orochi}}.]]Declaring himself winner of the trial, Susanoo then began to wreak havoc upon Takagamahara,<ref>Chamberlain (1882). [http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj022.htm Section XV.—The August Ravages of His Impetuous-Male-Augustness.]</ref><ref>{{cite wikisource |Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |chapter=Book I |author=Aston |date=1896 |pages=40–41}}</ref> causing Amaterasu to hide herself in the [[Amano-Iwato|Ama-no-Iwato]], plunging heaven and earth into darkness.<ref>Chamberlain (1882). [http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj023.htm Section XVI.—The Door of the Heavenly Rock-Dwelling.]</ref><ref>{{cite wikisource |Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |chapter=Book I |author=Aston |date=1896 |pages=41–45}}</ref> Though Amaterasu was eventually persuaded to come out of the cave, Susanoo was banished a second time as punishment for his misdeeds.<ref>Chamberlain (1882). [http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj024.htm Section XVII.—The August Expulsion of His-Impetuous-Male-Augustness.]</ref><ref>{{cite wikisource |Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |chapter=Book I |author=Aston |date=1896 |pages=45–52}}</ref> He then came down to [[:en:Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni|Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni]] (the 'Central Land of Reed Plains', i.e. the earthly land of Japan), to the {{ill|Izumo Province|en|Izumo Province|qid=Q582846|lt=land of Izumo|1=Izumo Province}}, where he slew the eight-headed serpent {{ill|Yamata no Orochi|en|Yamata no Orochi|qid=Q1054437|lt=Yamata-no-Orochi|1=Yamata no Orochi}} and married [[Kushinadahime|Kushinada-hime]]. At length, Susanoo went to the underworld ({{ill|Yomi|en|Yomi|qid=Q1142558|lt=Ne-no-kuni|1=Yomi}}) to become its ruler.<ref>Chamberlain (1882). [http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj024.htm Section XVIII.—The Eight-Forked Serpent.]</ref><ref>{{cite wikisource |Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |chapter=Book I |author=Aston |date=1896 |pages=45–63}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=Matsunaga|first1=Naomichi|title=Yamatanoorochi|url=http://k-amc.kokugakuin.ac.jp/DM/dbSearchList.do;jsessionid=734512D3512087B5065364047A4C4B03?class_name=col_eos&search_condition_type=1&db_search_condition_type=0&View=0&focus_type=0&startNo=1&searchFreeword=Orochi&searchRangeType=0|website=Encyclopedia of Shinto|publisher=Kokugakuin University}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=Mori|first1=Mizue|title=Kushinadahime|url=http://k-amc.kokugakuin.ac.jp/DM/dbSearchList.do;jsessionid=734512D3512087B5065364047A4C4B03?class_name=col_eos&search_condition_type=1&db_search_condition_type=0&View=0&focus_type=0&startNo=1&searchFreeword=Kushinadahime&searchRangeType=0|website=Encyclopedia of Shinto|publisher=Kokugakuin University}}</ref>

A son (''Nihon Shoki'') or descendant (''Kojiki'') of Susanoo, Ōnamuji,<ref>{{cite wikisource |Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |chapter=Book I |author=Aston |date=1896 |page=54}}</ref><ref>Chamberlain (1882). [http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj027.htm Section XX.—The August Ancestors of the Deity-Master-Of-The-Great Land.]</ref> married the goddess Yagami-hime of {{ill|Inaba Province|en|Inaba Province|qid=Q1054338|lt=Inaba Province|1=Inaba Province}}, earning the jealousy of his eighty brothers, who were seeking for her hand in marriage. Seeking refuge in Ne-no-kuni after his brothers had made attempts on his life,<ref>Chamberlain (1882). [http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj029.htm Section XXII.—Mount Tema.]</ref> Ōnamuji met Susanoo's daughter Suseri-bime, with whom he immediately fell in love with. Upon learning of their affair, Susanoo imposes four trials on Ōnamuji, each of which he overcame with Suseri-bime's help. Taking his new wife Suseri-bime, as well as Susanoo's sword, ''{{ill|Koto (instrument)|en|Koto (instrument)|qid=Q289037|lt=koto|1=Koto (instrument)}}'', and bow and arrow back with him, Ōnamuji – now called [[Ōkuninushi]] (大国主 'Master of the Great Land') – defeats his wicked brothers, thereby becoming the lord of Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni.<ref>Chamberlain (1882). [http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj030.htm Section XXIII.—The Nether-Distant-Land.]</ref>

Upon subduing his brothers, Ōkuninushi takes a third wife, Nunakawa-hime of {{ill|Koshi Province (Japan)|en|Koshi Province (Japan)|qid=Q1351611|lt=Koshi|1=Koshi Province (Japan)}},<ref>Chamberlain (1882). [http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj031.htm Section XXIV.—The Wooing of the Deity-of-Eight-Thousand-Spears.]</ref> causing his second (now chief) wife Suseri-bime to become jealous.<ref>Chamberlain (1882). [http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj032.htm Section XXV.—The Cup Pledge.]</ref> Ōkuninushi then begins the task of creating the land (''kuni-zukuri'') started by Izanagi and Izanami, being helped in his task by a dwarf named [[Sukunabikona|Sukunahikona]], a son of the [[Kotoamatsukami|primordial deity]] [[Takamimusubi]] (''Nihon Shoki'') or Kamimusubi (''Kojiki''). Together they made the lands habitable and invented means of dispelling various diseases and calamities such as [[medicine]] and [[Magic (paranormal)|magic]].<ref>Chamberlain (1882). [http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj034.htm Section XXVII.—The Little-Prince-the-Renowned-Deity.]</ref><ref>{{cite wikisource |Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |chapter=Book I |author=Aston |date=1896 |pages=59–60, 63}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=Kadoya|first1=Atsushi|title=Sukunahikona|url=http://k-amc.kokugakuin.ac.jp/DM/dbSearchList.do?class_name=col_eos&search_condition_type=1&db_search_condition_type=4&View=2&startNo=1&focus_type=0&searchFreeword=Sukunahikona&searchRangeType=0|website=Encyclopedia of Shinto|publisher=Kokugakuin University}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Merriam-Webster's Encyclopedia of World Religions|date=1999|publisher=Merriam-Webster|isbn=978-0877790440|page=[https://archive.org/details/isbn_9780877790440/page/824 824]|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/isbn_9780877790440/page/824}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Ashkenazi|first=Michael|title=Handbook of Japanese Mythology|url=https://archive.org/details/handbookofjapane0000ashk|url-access=registration|date=2003|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=978-1-57607-467-1|pages=[https://archive.org/details/handbookofjapane0000ashk/page/256 256]}}</ref>

==Plot==

===Ame-no-oshihomimi===
In time, the ''amatsukami'' of Takagamahara, headed by Amaterasu or/and Takamimusubi, decided that Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni, considered to be overpopulated by unruly and evil ''kami'', must be turned over to them to be pacified.<ref name="Nihongi64">{{cite wikisource |Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |chapter=Book II |author=Aston |date=1896 |page=64}}</ref> Amaterasu decreed that Ame-no-oshihomimi (天忍穂耳命),{{efn|This god's full name is ''Masaka(tsu)-Akatsu-Kachihayahi-Ame-no-oshihomimi-no-mikoto'' (正勝吾勝勝速日天忍穂耳(之)命, 正哉吾勝勝速日天忍穂耳尊).}} one of the five sons born to Amaterasu when Susanoo chewed her ''magatama'' beads, shall take possession of the earth and ordered him to go down to it. {{ill|Ame-no-oshihomimi|en|Ame-no-oshihomimi|qid=Q462555|lt=Ame-no-oshihomimi|1=Ame-no-oshihomimi}}, inspecting the land below from the bridge connecting heaven and earth, deemed it to be too tumultuous and refused to go any further, instead going back to report what he saw.<ref name="ChamberlainSectionXXX">Chamberlain (1882). [http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj037.htm Section XXX.—The August Deliberation for Pacifying the Land.]</ref>

[[File:Izumo-taisha 121281970 6d0f93bcde o.jpg|thumb|left|Ōkuninushi meeting the [[Hare of Inaba]], who helped him win the hand of Yagami-hime in exchange for his kindness towards it.]]

===Ame-no-hohi===
The heavenly gods then decided to send another of Amaterasu's sons, [[Ame no Hohi]] (天菩比神, 天穂日命), the most heroic among the gods, down to  Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni. Ame-no-hohi, however, began to curry favor with Ōkuninushi and did not send back any report for three years.<ref name="ChamberlainSectionXXX" /><ref name="Nihongi64" />

The ''Nihon Shoki'' adds that Ame-no-hohi's son, Ōsobi-no-mikuma-no-ushi (大背飯三熊之大人) was sent afterwards, but like his father, he did not report back to Takamagahara.<ref name="Nihongi6465">{{cite wikisource |Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |chapter=Book II |author=Aston |date=1896 |pages=64–65}}</ref>

===Ame-no-wakahiko===
After Ame-no-hohi's failure to return, the ''amatsukami'' sent another messenger, [[Ame no Wakahiko]] (天若日子, 天稚彦). However, he too came to side with Ōkuninushi, even marrying his daughter Shitateru-hime (下照比売命, 下照姫). After eight years of waiting, the heavenly deities sent a female [[:en:Japanese green pheasant|pheasant]] to question Ame-no-wakahiko, but he shot it with his bow and arrow at the prodding of a goddess named Ame-no-sagume (天佐具売, 天探女). The blood-stained arrow flew straight up to Takamagahara at the feet of [[Amaterasu]] and [[Takamimusubi]], who threw it back to earth with a curse, killing Ame-no-wakahiko.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Mori|first1=Mizue|title=Amewakahiko|url=http://eos.kokugakuin.ac.jp/modules/xwords/entry.php?entryID=46|website=Encyclopedia of Shinto|publisher=Kokugakuin University|access-date=13 February 2017}}</ref>

Ame-no-wakahiko's relatives, hearing the wailing of his bereaved wife, erect a mortuary house (喪屋 ''moya'') for Ame-no-wakahiko's corpse at the place where he died (''Kojiki'') or at Takamagahara (''Nihon Shoki''). They then celebrated his memory with song and dance for eight days and nights. A friend of Ame-no-wakahiko during his time on the earth who closely resembled him in appearance, [[Ajisukitakahikone|Ajishiki-/Ajisuki-takahikone]] (阿遅志貴高日子根神, 味耜高彦根神), went to attend Ame-no-wakahiko's funeral. Taking offense at being confused with the dead god by the family of the deceased, Ajisuki-takahikone destroyed the funeral house they built for Ame-no-wakahiko.<ref>Chamberlain (1882). [http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj038.htm Section XXXI.—The Heavenly-Young-Prince.]</ref><ref>{{cite wikisource |Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |chapter=Book II |author=Aston |date=1896 |pages=65–67}}</ref>

===Takemikazuchi===
{{Main|Takemikazuchi}}
[[File:Bentenjima on Inasa Beach.jpg|250px|thumb|right|Inasa Beach ([[:ja:稲佐の浜|稲佐の浜]] ''Inasa-no-hama'') in {{ill|Izumo|en|Izumo|qid=Q301580|lt=Izumo|1=Izumo}}, {{ill|Shimane Prefecture|en|Shimane Prefecture|qid=Q132751|lt=Shimane Prefecture|1=Shimane Prefecture}}, where the myth places Ōkuninushi's meeting with the messengers of heaven and his surrender to them.]]
After Ame-no-wakahiko's death, the gods of heaven convened another assembly to decide about whom to send next. In the ''Kojiki'', the selected candidates were the god Itsu-no-ohabari (the [[Totsuka-no-Tsurugi|sword]] Izanagi used to slay the fire god [[Kagu-tsuchi|Kagutsuchi]], the birth of whom caused Izanami's death) and his son, [[Takemikazuchi]].<ref>Chamberlain (1882). [http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj015.htm Section VIII.—The Slaying of the Fire-Deity.]</ref> As Itsu-no-ohabari was busy damming the headwaters of the heavenly river, Takemikazuchi, accompanied by the bird-boat deity [[Kamiumi#Birth of the gods|Ame-no-torifune]], was sent instead. In the ''Nihon Shoki'', meanwhile, the gods choose the sword god [[Futsunushi]] as their messenger; Takemikazuchi is chosen as his companion after he indignantly demanded to be sent as well.

The two messengers arrive at the shores of Inasa (伊那佐之小浜 ''Inasa no ohama''; ''Kojiki'') or Itasa (五十田狹之小汀 ''Itasa no ohama''; ''Nihon Shoki'') in the land of Izumo (modern {{ill|Taisha, Shimane|en|Taisha, Shimane|qid=Q7676403|lt=Taisha-machi|1=Taisha, Shimane}}, {{ill|Izumo|en|Izumo|qid=Q301580|lt=Izumo|1=Izumo}}, {{ill|Shimane Prefecture|en|Shimane Prefecture|qid=Q132751|lt=Shimane Prefecture|1=Shimane Prefecture}}). Sitting on the points of their upturned swords, they questioned Ōkuninushi what his intentions were with regard to the land, which was the possession of Amaterasu's descendants. Ōkuninushi asked to confer with his son [[Kotoshironushi-no-Mikoto|Kotoshironushi]] first before giving his decision. Kotoshironushi, who had gone hunting and fishing, immediately acceded to the messengers' demands. After counseling his father to do likewise, he then disappeared.<ref name="Chamberlain">Chamberlain (1882). [http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj039.htm Section XXXII.—Abdication of the Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land.]</ref><ref name="Nihongi6869">{{cite wikisource |Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |chapter=Book II |author=Aston |date=1896 |pages=68–69}}</ref>

The ''Kojiki'' adds that a younger son of Ōkuninushi, [[Takeminakata]], carrying a giant boulder on the fingertips of a single hand, challenged Takemikazuchi to a test of strength. When Takeminakata tried to seize Takemikazuchi's arm, the latter transformed it into an icicle and then a sword blade, preventing Takeminakata from grabbing it. When Takemikazuchi grasped Takeminakata's arm in return, he crushed it like a reed and threw it aside. Pursued by Takemikazuchi, the injured Takeminakata fled to "the {{ill|Lake Suwa|en|Lake Suwa|qid=Q1206692|lt=sea of Suwa|1=Lake Suwa}} in the {{ill|Shinano Province|en|Shinano Province|qid=Q289250|lt=province of Shinano|1=Shinano Province}}" (科野国州羽海), where he pleaded for his life and surrendered, vowing not to leave Shinano.<ref name="Chamberlain" /><ref name="Hackin1932">{{cite book|author=J. Hackin|title=Asiatic Mythology: A Detailed Description and Explanation of the Mythologies of All the Great Nations of Asia|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HAZrFhvqnTkC&pg=PA395|year=1932|publisher=Asian Educational Services|isbn=978-81-206-0920-4|page=395}}</ref><ref name="Herbert2010">{{cite book|author=Jean Herbert|title=Shinto: At the Fountainhead of Japan|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Sg_JBQAAQBAJ&pg=PT437|date=18 October 2010|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-136-90376-2|page=437}}</ref><ref name="Ashkenazi2003">Ashkenazi (2003). pp. 267–268.</ref>

With Kotoshironushi's counsel (and Takeminakata's surrender), Ōkuninushi finally agreed to cede the land to the descendants of Amaterasu. 
As a condition, he asked that [[Izumo-taisha|a magnificent palace]] – rooted in the earth and reaching up to heaven – be built for him on Tagishi beach (多芸志之小浜 ''Tagishi no ohama'') in Izumo, where special foods from the sea will be offered (''Kojiki'').<ref name="Chamberlain" /> Bequeathing a broad spear he used to pacify the land to the two divine messengers (''Nihon Shoki''), Ōkuninushi disappeared and became the ruler of the unseen world.<ref name="shinto-encyclopedia"/><ref name="Nihongi6970">{{cite wikisource |Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |chapter=Book II |author=Aston |date=1896 |pages=69–70}}</ref>

After Ōkuninushi's assent and withdrawal, the two messengers proceeded to destroy everyone and everything who refused to submit to their authority. They then send the god of weaving, {{ill|Takehazuchi|ja|天羽槌雄神|1=Takehazuchi|2=ja|3=天羽槌雄神|4=zh|5=天羽槌雄神|6=fr|7=Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takehazuchi|13=User:Immanuelle/Takehazuchi|qq=}} (建葉槌), to subdue the star god [[Amatsu-Mikaboshi|Kagaseo]] (香香背男), the last remaining rebel against Takamagahara (''Nihon Shoki'').<ref name="Nihongi6970" /> With all resistance finally gone, the two gods went back to heaven to report the success of their mission.

====Alternate version====

A third version of the story also found in the ''Nihon Shoki'' has Kagaseo – here given the alternative name Amatsu-mikaboshi (天津甕星) – being put to death in Takamagahara by Futsunushi and Takemikazuchi before they descend to Izumo. In this version, Ōkuninushi – as Ōnamochi (大己貴神), the name used for the god in the ''Nihon Shoki'' – initially refuses the demand of the two envoys. After Futsunushi goes back to Takamagahara to report, Takamimusubi sends the two messengers back to Ōnamochi, this time with promises of rewards should he comply: in exchange for his political authority, he (Ōnamochi) will be given authority over religious matters, a magnificent palace to dwell in, and festivals in his honor presided by Amaterasu's son Ame-no-hohi. Finding these too good to refuse, Ōnamochi finally accepts their terms. Introducing the god of roads and borders, [[:en:Kunado-No-Kami|Kunado-/Funado-no-kami]] (岐神) to the envoys as his replacement, Ōnamochi disappears into the unseen world.

Appointing Kunado-no-kami as guide, Futsunushi proceeds to go around Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni, slaying those who resisted him and rewarding those who rendered obedience. The now-invisible Ōnamochi, under the name [[Ōmononushi]] (大物主), and Kotoshironushi go up to Takamagahara to swear fealty to the gods of heaven. Takamimusubi rewards Ōnamochi/Ōmononushi by giving him his daughter Mihotsu-hime (三穂津姫) as his wife, and sends him back to earth with "the eighty myriads of deities."<ref>{{cite wikisource |Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |chapter=Book II |author=Aston |date=1896 |pages=79–80}}</ref>

===Aftermath===
{{see also|Tenson kōrin}}

The earth now under their possession, the ''amatsukami'' sent the "Heavenly Grandson" (天孫 ''tenson''), Ame-no-oshihomimi's son [[Ninigi-no-Mikoto|Ninigi]], to rule over Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni,<ref>Chamberlain (1882). [http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj040.htm Section XXXIII.—The August Descent from Heaven of His Augustness the August Grandchild.]</ref> bearing with him the {{ill|Imperial Regalia of Japan|en|Imperial Regalia of Japan|qid=Q327465|lt=three sacred treasures|1=Imperial Regalia of Japan}}: the sword ([[Kusanagi no Tsurugi]]), the mirror ([[Yata no Kagami]]), and the jewel ([[Yasakani no Magatama]]). Ninigi, taking the goddess [[Konohanasakuya-hime|Konohana-sakuya-hime]] as his wife,<ref>Chamberlain (1882). [http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj041.htm Section XXXIV.—The August Reign in Himuka of His Augustness Prince Rice-Ear-Ruddy-Plenty.]</ref> eventually became the ancestor of the {{ill|Imperial House of Japan|en|Imperial House of Japan|qid=Q909452|lt=emperors of Japan|1=Imperial House of Japan}}.<ref>{{cite wikisource |Nihongi: Chronicles of Japan from the Earliest Times to A.D. 697 |chapter=Book II |author=Aston |date=1896 |pages=70–92}}</ref>

==Similar myths==

In addition to the Izumo myth cycle recorded in the official histories, other sources provide stories with a similar theme: the transfer of power from one god to another.

===Ise: Isetsuhiko===
{{see also|Isetsuhiko}}

The ''[[Fudoki]]'' of {{ill|Ise Province|en|Ise Province|qid=Q864166|lt=Ise Province|1=Ise Province}}, which survives only in excerpts quoted in other writings, relates the story of an obscure god of the wind, [[Isetsuhiko]], who was said to have surrendered his land (what would become Ise) to Amenohiwake-no-mikoto (天日別命), who claimed it in the name of Ninigi's great-grandson {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|en|Emperor Jimmu|qid=Q200188|lt=Jimmu|1=Emperor Jimmu}}, who launched a military campaign to conquer the eastern lands of Japan.<ref>{{cite web|title=''Manyoshu chūshaku'', vol. 1 (萬葉集註釋 卷第一)|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/2575769/32|author=Sengaku|author-link=Sengaku}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Kurita|first1=Hiroshi|title=Kofudoki itsubun (古風土記逸文)|date=1927|publisher=Ōokayama-shoten|pages=33–37|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YKK4vAbajRQC}}</ref><ref name="Fudoki">{{cite web|title=伊勢國風土記逸文|url=http://miko.org/~uraki/kuon/furu/text/fuudo/itubun/itubun01.htm}}</ref> Isetsuhiko is himself apparently identified as the son of a god hailing from Izumo, hence his other name Izumonotakeko-no-mikoto (出雲建子命).<ref name="Fudoki" /><ref>Kurita (1927). pp. 44–45.</ref>

===Suwa: Moreya===
{{see also|Moreya|Suwa taisha}}

Local myths in the Suwa region of {{ill|Shinano Province|en|Shinano Province|qid=Q289250|lt=Shinano|1=Shinano Province}} (modern {{ill|Nagano Prefecture|en|Nagano Prefecture|qid=Q127877|lt=Nagano Prefecture|1=Nagano Prefecture}}) speak of a foreign deity who was challenged upon his arrival in Suwa by a local god named [[Moriya|Moreya]]. After subduing Moreya and other ''kami'' who resisted him, the outsider finally established himself as the region's chief god, being enshrined at the [[Suwa-taisha|Suwa Grand Shrine]] by the shores of {{ill|Lake Suwa|en|Lake Suwa|qid=Q1206692|lt=Lake Suwa|1=Lake Suwa}}.<ref name="Moriya">Moriya, Sanae (1991). ''Moriya-jinchō-ke no ohanashi'' (守矢神長家のお話し). In Jinchōkan Moriya Historical Museum (Ed.). ''Jinchōkan Moriya Shiryōkan no shiori'' (神長官守矢資料館のしおり) (Rev. ed.). pp. 2–3.</ref><ref>Miyasaka, Mitsuaki (1987). "Kyodai naru kami no kuni. Suwa-shinkō no tokushitsu (強大なる神の国―諏訪信仰の特質)." In Miyasaka, Mitsuaki (1987). "Kyodai naru kami no kuni. Suwa-shinkō no tokushitsu (強大なる神の国―諏訪信仰の特質)." In {{cite book|author1=Ueda|author2=Gorai|author3=Ōbayashi|author4=Miyasaka, M.|author5=Miyasaka, Y.|title=御柱祭と諏訪大社 (Onbashira-sai to Suwa-taisha)|date=1987 |location=Nagano|publisher=Chikuma Shobō|isbn=978-4480841810|pages=21–22}}</ref><ref name="呉清恵2011">{{cite book|author=Oh, Amana ChungHae|title=Cosmogonical Worldview of Jomon Pottery|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hxulspIN_2UC&pg=PA157-158|date=2011|publisher=Sankeisha|isbn=978-4-88361-924-5|pages=155–164}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|editor1-last=Yazaki|editor1-first=Takenori|title=Suwa-taisha (諏訪大社)|date=1986|publisher=Ginga shobō|series=Ginga gurafikku sensho|volume=4|pages=24–25}}</ref> This god, usually known as Suwa-{{ill|Myōjin|en|Myōjin|qid=Q5369590|lt=Myōjin|1=Myōjin}} (諏訪明神), is most commonly identified with the ''Kojiki''<nowiki />'s Takeminakata.<ref name="Moriya" />

==Analysis==

It is believed that the two earliest official chronicles, the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Nihon Shoki'', which purport to contain the 'correct' early history of Japan, were compiled as propaganda designed to legitimize the rule and increase the prestige of the {{ill|Imperial House of Japan|en|Imperial House of Japan|qid=Q909452|lt=imperial dynasty|1=Imperial House of Japan}}, which claimed descent from Amaterasu via Ninigi.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Turnbull|first1=Stephen|title=The Samurai and the Sacred: The Path of the Warrior|date=2011|publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing|isbn=978-1849089944|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6uPvCwAAQBAJ&pg=PT16|page=16}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Yamato: Glossary & Characters|website=Office of Resources for International and Area Studies (ORIAS)|url=http://orias.berkeley.edu/sites/default/files/yamato_glossary.pdf}}</ref> As such, the Izumo ''kuni-yuzuri'' cycle has often been interpreted as a mythic retelling and justification of the rise to power of the Yamato state and its subjugation of other clans and tribes,<ref name="shinto-encyclopedia"/><ref>{{cite book|last1=Dolan|first1=Ronald E.|last2=Worden|first2=Robert L.|title=Japan: A Country Study|date=1992|publisher=Federal Research Division, Library of Congress|location=Washington, D.C.|isbn=978-0-8444-0731-9|pages=[https://archive.org/details/japancountrystud00dola/page/5 5–6]|url=https://archive.org/details/japancountrystud00dola/page/5}}</ref> such as those of Izumo (represented by its deities).<ref name="Ashkenazi2003" /><ref>{{cite book|last1=Plutschow|first1=Herbert|title=Matsuri: The Festivals of Japan|date=1996|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-873410-63-9|page=23|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AYX7AQAAQBAJ&pg=PA23}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Zhong|first1=Yijiang|title=The Origin of Modern Shinto in Japan: The Vanquished Gods of Izumo|date=2016|publisher=Bloomsbury Academic|isbn=978-1-4742-7108-0|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LrrMDAAAQBAJ&pg=PT207}}</ref><ref name="Henshall">{{cite book|last1=Henshall|first1=Kenneth|title=A History of Japan: From Stone Age to Superpower|date=2012|publisher=Palgrave Macmillan|isbn=978-0-230-34662-8|pages=15–16|edition=3rd|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vD76fF5hqf8C&pg=PA16}}</ref>

===Futsunushi and Takemikazuchi===

Both the ''Kojiki'' and the ''Nihon Shoki'' agree in naming one of the two messengers the gods of Takamagahara send to Ōkuninushi to be Takemikazuchi, the god of [[Kashima Jingū|Kashima Shrine]] in {{ill|Hitachi Province|en|Hitachi Province|qid=Q1055353|lt=Hitachi Province|1=Hitachi Province}} (modern {{ill|Ibaraki Prefecture|en|Ibaraki Prefecture|qid=Q83273|lt=Ibaraki Prefecture|1=Ibaraki Prefecture}}) who was worshipped by the influential [[Nakatomi clan]], which oversaw the religious rituals of the imperial court, and its offshoot, the [[Fujiwara clan]].<ref name="Matsumae">{{cite book|author=Matsumae, Takeshi|title=Nihon shinwa no nazo ga yoku wakaru hon (日本神話の謎がよく分かる本)|date=2007|publisher=Daiwa Shobō (大和書房)|isbn=978-4-479-39166-1|pages=136–137}}</ref><ref name="Tobe">{{cite book|last1=Tobe|first1=Tamio|title=「日本の神様」がよくわかる本 ("Nihon no kami-sama" ga yoku yakaru hon)|date=2004|publisher=PHP Kenkyujo|isbn=978-4-569-66115-5|page=57|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CK27BQAAQBAJ&pg=PT57}}</ref><ref>Miyasaka (1987). pp. 18–20.</ref> The second messenger meanwhile is identified in the ''Nihon Shoki'' as [[Futsunushi|Futsunushi-no-kami]] (経津主神), the deity of [[Katori Jingū|Katori Shrine]] in {{ill|Shimōsa Province|en|Shimōsa Province|qid=Q1053695|lt=Shimōsa Province|1=Shimōsa Province}} (modern {{ill|Chiba Prefecture|en|Chiba Prefecture|qid=Q80011|lt=Chiba Prefecture|1=Chiba Prefecture}}) worshipped by the [[Mononobe clan]].<ref name="Futsunushi">{{cite web|last1=Kadoya|first1=Atsushi|title=Futsunushi|url=http://k-amc.kokugakuin.ac.jp/DM/dbSearchList.do;jsessionid=FD1D80CB7487CDB06FD062C635333588?class_name=col_eos&search_condition_type=1&db_search_condition_type=0&View=0&focus_type=0&startNo=1&searchFreeword=Futsunushi&searchRangeType=0|website=Encyclopedia of Shinto|publisher=Kokugakuin University}}</ref>

While in the ''Kojiki'' it is Takemikazuchi among the two messengers who takes center stage, the two versions of the myth found in ''Nihon Shoki'' and other sources imply that the central role was originally occupied by Futsunushi. For instance, both the ''[[Fudoki]]'' of Izumo Province and the ''Izumo-no-kuni-no-miyatsuko-no-kanyogoto'' (Izumo Province 造神賀詞 "Divine Congratulatory Words of the ''Kuni-no-Miyatsuko'' of Izumo"), an address the chieftain or governor ([[kuni no miyatsuko|''kuni-no-miyatsuko''/''kokuzō'']]) of Izumo offered to the {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|qid=Q208233|lt=Emperor|1=Emperor of Japan}} on behalf of Izumo's deities as a sign of his allegiance to the imperial court,<ref>{{cite book|author1=Breen, John|author2=Teeuwen, Mark|title=Shinto in History: Ways of the Kami|date=2013|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1136826979|pages=62–63|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DR2PAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA63}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Bocking|first1=Brian|title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto|date=2005|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1135797393|page=166|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6d-RAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA166}}</ref> mention or imply only Futsunushi (recorded in both texts as 布都怒志命/布都努志命 ''Futsunushi-no-mikoto'') as descending from heaven, with no mention of Takemikazuchi.<ref>{{cite web|title=Izumo-no-kuni-no-miyatsuko-no-kanyogoto (出雲國造神賀詞)|url=http://miko.org/~uraki/kuon/furu/text/rituryou/engi/engi.htm|website=Engishiki (延喜式)}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|editor=Shimane-ken Kōten Kōkyū Bunsho|title=Izumo-no-kuni Fudoki (出雲國風土記)|date=1929|publisher=Shimane-ken Kōten Kōkyū Bunsho|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1186554/19}}</ref> It is therefore thought that Takemikazuchi gradually came to take on Futsunushi's attributes and roles, coinciding with the decline of the Mononobe and the rise of the Nakatomi.<ref name="Futsunushi" /><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Murayama|first1=Naoko|title=フツヌシ神話と物部氏|journal=Gakushuin University Studies in Humanities|date=2000|issue=9|pages=103–121|url=http://ci.nii.ac.jp/naid/110000545959}}</ref>

[[File:Ono-Yasumaro.jpg|thumb|right|{{ill|Ō no Yasumaro|en|Ō no Yasumaro|qid=Q384705|lt=Ō no Yasumaro|1=Ō no Yasumaro}}, compiler and editor of the ''[[Kojiki]]''.]]

===Takeminakata===

Takeminakata's abrupt appearance in the ''Kojiki''<nowiki />'s version of the myth has long puzzled scholars, as the god is mentioned nowhere else in the work, including the genealogy of Ōkuninushi's progeny that precedes the ''kuni-yuzuri'' narrative proper.<ref>Chamberlain (1882). [http://sacred-texts.com/shi/kj/kj033.htm Section XXVI.—The Deities the August Descendants of the Deity Master-of-the-Great-Land.]</ref> Aside from the ''[[:en:Sendai Kuji Hongi|Sendai Kuji Hongi]]'' (aka the ''Kujiki''), which nearly-verbatim replicates the ''Kojiki''<nowiki />'s ''kuni-yuzuri'' narrative and adds the information that Takeminakata is a son of Nunakawa-hime,<ref>先代舊事本紀 巻第四 (''Sendai Kuji Hongi'', book 4), in {{cite book|editor=Keizai Zasshisha|title=国史大系 第7巻 (Kokushi-taikei, vol. 7)|date=1898|publisher=Keizai Zasshisha|pages=243–244|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/991097/136}}</ref> he is altogether absent from the ''Nihon Shoki'' as well as from early sources dealing with Izumo such as the province's ''Fudoki''.

While earlier authors tended to explain this absence by equating Takeminakata with certain minor deities who are thought to share certain parallels with him (e.g. Isetsuhiko), claiming that these were actually Takeminakata under a different name,<ref name="Norinaga2">Motoori, Norinaga (1937). [http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/1109355/81 古事記傳 (''Kojiki-den''), vol. 14] in Motoori Toyokai (ed.), 本居宣長全集 (''Motoori Norinaga Zenshū''), vol. 2. Tokyo: Yoshikawa Kōbunkan. pp. 683–684. (Original work written 1764–1798)</ref> more recent scholars suggest instead that the god was an original invention by the ''Kojiki'''s compilers, who, for one reason or another, then grafted him to the Izumo myth cycle.<ref name="Yoshii">{{Citation|title = Takeminakata-no-kami (建御名方神)|author=Yoshii, Iwao|encyclopedia = Encyclopedia Nipponica|date=1994 |volume=14|publisher=Shōgakukan|isbn=978-4-09-526114-0}}.</ref><ref name="Matsumae"/>

Due to Takeminakata being associated with the Suwa region in historical {{ill|Shinano Province|en|Shinano Province|qid=Q289250|lt=Shinano Province|1=Shinano Province}} (modern {{ill|Nagano Prefecture|en|Nagano Prefecture|qid=Q127877|lt=Nagano Prefecture|1=Nagano Prefecture}}), scholars look for his origin in this area. It is believed that the ''Kojiki''<nowiki/>'s chief compiler, {{ill|Ō no Yasumaro|en|Ō no Yasumaro|qid=Q384705|lt=Ō no Yasumaro|1=Ō no Yasumaro}}, might have created 'Takeminakata' based on either local legends or recent history (cf. Moreya's resistance against Suwa-myōjin, thought to be a mythicization of local resistance against the encroachment of the [[:en:Yamato state|Yamato state]] on the Suwa area) and/or the indigenous pre-Yamato belief system revolving around the {{ill|en:List of nature deities|en|en:List of nature deities|qid=Q6630292|lt=nature god(s)|1=List of nature deities}} [[Mishaguji]] and the subsequent adaptation and reorganization of that system under Yamato rule.<ref>Miyasaka (1987). pp. 17–26.</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Ōwa|first1=Iwao|title=信濃古代史考 (Shinano Kodai Shikō)|date=1990|publisher=Meicho Shuppan|location=Tokyo|isbn=978-4626013637|pages=212–214}}</ref><ref name="呉清恵2011" /><ref>{{cite book|editor=Suwa Shishi Hensan Iinkai|title=諏訪市史 上巻 原始・古代・中世 (Suwa-shi Shi (History of Suwa City), vol. 1: Genshi, Kodai, Chūsei)|date=1995|location=Suwa|pages=687–689|url=http://dl.ndl.go.jp/info:ndljp/pid/9572217}}</ref> Scholars point out Yasumaro's clan, the Ō, being distantly related to the clan of the ''kuni-no-miyatsuko'' of Shinano, the authorities set up by the imperial court to govern the area, as one possible motivation for inventing a new god based on the legends, the religious practices and the history of Suwa.<ref>Miyasaka (1987). p. 19.</ref>
